source.title: Towards Universality: Studying Mechanistic Similarity Across Language Model Architectures
source.authors: Junxuan Wang; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Qiong Tang; Yunhua Zhou; Zheng-Fu He; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: It tests representational and feature similarity across architectures and random seeds using SAE-feature matching and maximum pairwise Pearson correlation, rather than reproducing the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cross-model SAE-feature similarity and seed comparisons. It also gives a qualitative induction-circuit analogy, but does not directly test a Transformer circuit in this study; the Transformer comparison draws on prior work. The paper's GPT-4o scoring prompts are quoted evaluation prompts, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewing this text.
record.test_reason: The study measures SAE-feature recurrence across Pythia, Mamba and RWKV, and across Pythia seeds, using max pairwise Pearson correlation. That is a different method aimed at whether the same features recur across models (V5) and across seeds (V3). It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors propose MPPC minus the seed-skyline MPPC as a measure of architectural effect, and read lower MPPC as partly reflecting feature complexity rather than non-universality. They flag that SAEs capture only a subset of features and that circuit universality is qualitative.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE decomposition and maximum pairwise Pearson correlation to compare feature activations, plus circuit path patching; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods or test convergence as model scale and capability increase.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported MPPC depends on feature complexity and matching direction. The reverse Pythia–Mamba direction has a higher mean than the forward direction; feature matching also shows layer-depth structure.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4o monosemanticity scores split MPPC at about 0.2: features below that are mostly uninterpretable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low cross-model match scores mark uninterpretable or noise SAE features, so SAE-based similarity measures partly reflect feature quality.

record.problems: The main cross-architecture comparison involves only Pythia-160M and Mamba-130M, which share a tokenizer and Pile training data, so architecture is not isolated from those shared conditions. The paper notes that SAEs may capture only a subset of true features or combinations of features. Its main comparison uses one asymmetric similarity metric, and it reports no uncertainty estimates. The induction-circuit comparison is qualitative rather than quantitatively evaluated across both architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the paper's layer-by-layer path-patching logit-difference tables: those results identify components within Mamba and do not directly measure cross-model circuit recurrence. The Transformer-side circuit analogy is discussed qualitatively and draws on prior work rather than a direct Transformer experiment in this study.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep; the models are 130–169M and similarity is not related to performance.
No mapping, stitching or transfer-loss test between models.

Circuit recurrence is shown only qualitatively (induction analogy, with the Transformer side from prior work). There is no comparison across sizes or model families beyond three small Pile-trained LMs.
No alternative similarity metrics, neighbour settings, input distributions or out-of-distribution tests; only matching direction is varied.
Training data and tokenizer are shared and never varied, so the cause of the similarity is untested; no plateau test.

missing.what: MPPC difference distribution versus the seed skyline: 90% of features fall in -0.22 to 0.14, over 60% near zero (Mamba). For RWKV the interval is -0.45 to 0.06.
SAE seed skyline, mean MPPC 0.81 (upper bound on achievable similarity).
Cross-architecture MPPC shifts lower in deeper Pythia layers (groups 0–2 through 9–11).

Qualitative induction-circuit analogy: Mamba uses layer-17 SSM state plus convolution, analogous to previous-token and induction heads, with an off-by-one difference. This is a circuit-level V5 result, unquantified.

record.verdict_notes: All models are small and share Pile data; Pythia and Mamba also share a tokenizer. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The V7 label was removed because the study neither varies shared training conditions nor shows alignment far from complete; the cross-architecture mean is near the seed skyline.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model scale or capability; the main Pythia and Mamba models are near-sized, and similarity is not related to performance.
No vision-language model pair, paired images and captions, or cross-modal scaling/performance comparison.
Tests SAE-feature similarity for a Pythia model and a different-seed Pythia model, not whether the same individual units or bases recur.
Matches SAE features by activation correlation, but does not test whether one model's representations can be mapped to another's with low loss.

Tests SAE features across selected language-model architectures; does not test recurring neurons or SAE features across broad model families, sizes, or training settings. The circuit comparison is qualitative and not quantitatively evaluated across both models.
Reports dependence on feature complexity and matching direction for MPPC, but does not compare alternative similarity metrics or input distributions, or test out-of-distribution inputs.

Reports incomplete and architecture-dependent similarity and notes shared tokenizer/training data for the main pair, but does not test whether shared data or objectives cause the similarity, nor test a plateau.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M and Mamba-130M
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Matched each Pythia SAE feature to its most correlated Mamba SAE feature using MPPC

conditions.value: 12 Pythia layers and 24 Mamba layers; F=24576

rows.measure: Mean Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (Pythia to Mamba)
rows.value: 0.74 average; more than 30% of Pythia features have MPPC greater than 0.95; more than 60% have near-zero MPPC difference from the Pythia model-seed variant
rows.note: Aggregate result across Pythia features. Both models use the same tokenizer and are trained on the Pile; the paper does not isolate the contribution of this shared training setup.
rows.check: Drop the V7 link. Cross-architecture mean MPPC 0.74 is close to the seed skyline 0.76, and the study never varies or isolates shared data or tokenizer, so the row cannot speak to V7's causal claim. The value also folds in the Figure 3b difference distribution, which would be clearer as its own row.

rows.subject: Pythia MLP neurons and Mamba post-SiLU activations
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron/activation patterns across architectures using maximum pairwise Pearson correlation
rows.value: 0.30 average; described as showing almost no sign of similarity
rows.note: The authors present this as a neuron-basis baseline that is not informative for comparing the architectures.
rows.check: State should be absent, not partial. The paper says the neuron baseline (mean 0.30) 'almost exhibits zero sign of similarity'. Note that the authors treat Mamba post-SiLU activations as having no true neuron counterpart, so this is a baseline rather than a fair neuron-universality test.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M and a Pythia model trained with a different random seed
rows.stage_stated: Different random seed; training data order also differs
rows.operation_detail: Matched SAE features between same-architecture models using MPPC
rows.note: Aggregate result for the model-seed skyline.
rows.check: No problem. Different seed and data order, mean MPPC 0.76.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M and RWKV-169M
rows.stage_stated: Pythia trained on the Pile; RWKV-4-169M-Pile
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the cross-architecture SAE-feature matching experiment using MPPC
rows.note: The paper says the results largely support its conclusions, while noting the score is slightly lower than in the Mamba comparison.
rows.check: Evaluation data is probably the same OpenWebText setup ('nearly identical experiments'), not 'not stated'. Mean 0.65 is below the 0.76 seed skyline. The Figure 11b difference interval (-0.45 to 0.06) is wider and more negative than for Mamba.

source_check.problem: Appendix D describes nearly identical experiments but does not independently specify the evaluation dataset; lower MPPC does not isolate an architectural cause.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M and Mamba-130M
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Reversed the direction of maximum-feature matching
rows.note: The paper attributes the higher reverse-direction result primarily to Mamba having a larger proportion of lower-level, simpler features.
rows.check: For V5 the reverse direction is observed (0.78). For V6, reversing direction changes the mean by only +0.04 and convergence does not weaken or vanish, so the dependence is small.

source_check.correct: V5 state: observed, with reverse-direction mean MPPC 0.78. V6 state: partial, with a direction-dependent change from 0.74 to 0.78 and persistent strong correspondence.
source_check.problem: The single partial state conflates observed feature recurrence under V5 with modest direction dependence under V6.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M and a Pythia model trained with a different random seed
rows.stage_stated: Different random seed; training data order also differs
rows.operation_detail: Reversed the direction of maximum-feature matching
rows.note: The paper describes forward and reverse seed-variant results as very close.
rows.check: For V6 the state is absent: forward and reverse seed results are 0.76 and 0.75, which the paper calls very close. For V3 the 0.75 is observed.

source_check.correct: V3 state: observed, with reverse-direction mean MPPC 0.75. V6 state: absent for appreciable direction dependence; forward and reverse means are 0.76 and 0.75, described as very close.
source_check.problem: Absent fits negligible direction dependence under V6, but incorrectly describes the substantial cross-seed correspondence under V3.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M SAE features matched to Mamba-130M SAE features
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Related feature complexity scores to MPPC
rows.value: The paper reports a clear correlation: simpler Pythia features are more likely to have higher MPPC in the cross-architecture comparison
rows.note: The text describes the trend, but the plotted category-specific values are not stated.
rows.check: Relink from V6 to V5. Feature complexity is a property of which features recur, not of the similarity metric's settings or inputs. Complex features mostly match at MPPC 0.3–0.8, simple ones near 1, so recurrence is weaker for complex features. Figure-only; category values are not readable.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 5.1–5.2; Figure 5a and its following paragraph.
source_check.problem: Lower MPPC for complex features concerns activation correspondence; the authors caution that semantic themes can still agree.

rows.subject: Pythia SAE features matched to Mamba SAE features
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared MPPC with GPT-4o-scored feature monosemanticity
rows.value: The paper reports a clear boundary around MPPC 0.2; features below that threshold are highly likely to be uninterpretable
rows.note: The paper uses this result to connect low similarity scores with uninterpretable features; it does not compare alternative similarity metrics.
rows.check: This validates the metric: MPPC below about 0.2 marks uninterpretable features. It does not measure convergence under alternative metric choices, so it does not bear on V6. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pythia SAE features matched to Mamba SAE features
rows.stage_stated: Both trained on the Pile dataset
rows.operation_detail: Recorded the layer locations of maximum-correlation feature pairs
rows.measure: Layer distribution of best-matching feature pairs
rows.value: Matched pairs mainly occur at near-proportional depth; a Pythia feature at layer l is most likely matched around Mamba layer 2l
rows.note: The paper reports a qualitative depth-specialization pattern.
rows.check: No problem. Pythia layer l matches near Mamba layer 2l, and the same depth pattern holds in the reverse direction (Figure 10).

relation.reason: The study reports its own cross-architecture and cross-seed feature-correspondence experiments.

tranche.reason: SAE-feature matching and circuit path patching directly investigate recurring features and mechanisms using a different operational method.

source_check.notes: MPPC measures firing correspondence, and complexity can lower it despite shared semantic themes. SAEs capture only a subset of possible features; circuit similarity is qualitative, and shared training data/tokenizer effects are not isolated.

statements.correction: Pythia–RWKV mean MPPC: 0.65; Pythia–Mamba: 0.74; model-seed skyline: 0.76; neuron baseline: 0.30. RWKV's lower score may reflect SAE training or unknown factors. Complex matched features often have MPPC between 0.3 and 0.8 despite agreement in semantic theme.
statements.problem: The numerical comparisons are correct, but architecture-dependent recurrence is stronger than established: the authors explicitly decline to rank architectural similarity, and lower complex-feature MPPC need not imply weaker semantic recurrence.
